Bereave
bē-rēv´
v. (to deprive, especially of children; rendering Hebrew shakol)
From be- and reave, to plunder. To bereave is to have something taken by force rather than lost.

Biblical Definition

To bereave is to be deprived. Jacob says it twice at the lowest points of his life: “me have ye bereaved of my children: Joseph is not, and Simeon is not, and ye will take Benjamin away” (Gen 42:36), and later, “if I be bereaved of my children, I am bereaved” (Gen 43:14). Ezekiel speaks of a land that has bereaved its nations (Eze 36:13), and Hosea prays, “give them a miscarrying womb and dry breasts” in judgment (Hos 9:14).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines bereave as to deprive; to strip; to make destitute; and it is followed by of, and is used especially of the loss of friends by death.

expand to see more

BEREAVE, v.t. To deprive; to strip; to make destitute; with of before the thing taken away.

2. To take away from.

BEREAVEMENT, n. Deprivation, particularly by the loss of a friend by death.

Key Scripture

Gen 42:36 — "And Jacob their father said unto them, Me have ye bereaved of my children: Joseph is not, and Simeon is not, and ye will take Benjamin away: all these things are against me."

Gen 43:14 — "And God Almighty give you mercy before the man, that he may send away your other brother, and Benjamin. If I be bereaved of my children, I am bereaved."

Eze 36:13 — "Thus saith the Lord GOD; Because they say unto you, Thou land devourest up men, and hast bereaved thy nations;"

Gen 42:38 — "And he said, My son shall not go down with you; for his brother is dead, and he is left alone: if mischief befall him by the way in the which ye go, then shall ye bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the grave."

Modern Corruption

Grief is expected to reach acceptance, and Jacob's surrender in Genesis 43 is not peace but exhaustion — and God honoured it anyway.

expand to see more

Genesis 42:36 is one of the most human sentences in the Bible: all these things are against me. Jacob is wrong about every particular — Joseph is alive and governing Egypt, Simeon is safe, and Benjamin will return — and he could not possibly have known it. Scripture records the despair of a man reading his providence backwards, without correcting him in the moment.

Genesis 43:14 is his eventual surrender, and it is bleak rather than serene: and God Almighty give you mercy before the man, that he may send away your other brother, and Benjamin. If I be bereaved of my children, I am bereaved. He invokes God's name and then braces for the worst. That is faith at the end of its resources, and the chapter that follows is the beginning of everything being restored to him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shakol (H7921), to be bereaved of children, to miscarry; the same root used of a land bereaving its inhabitants.

expand to see more

Hebrew shakol (H7921) — to bereave, be childless; Genesis 42:36, 43:14, Ezekiel 36:13-14.

Hebrew El Shaddai — God Almighty; Genesis 43:14, the name Jacob invokes at his lowest.

Hebrew racham (H7356) — mercy, compassion; give you mercy before the man.

Usage

"“All these things are against me” — wrong about every particular, and recorded uncorrected."

"“If I be bereaved of my children, I am bereaved” — faith at the end of its resources."

"“God Almighty give you mercy before the man” — the name invoked at the lowest point."
